title: All formations pass
hookLine: the thing you made gets ruined: a verse that asks you to see before you do
tomorrow: which comes first, the bad mood or the bad day?

lines: A CAKE, A FILE, A SPILL.
cards: A cake you spent all afternoon on slides off the plate. A file you worked on for a week won't open. A drawing gets a glass of juice tipped across it.
Every one of those has a split second where your whole body says no. And yesterday's question waits right there: if all things pass, what are you meant to do about it?
Dhammapada two seventy-seven has an answer, and it may not be the one you expect. Its first move isn't to do anything. It's to see.

teach.b: The verse opens with today's line: sabbe sankhara anicca. All formations are impermanent. Sabbe, all, the same word as in yesterday's wish for all beings.
Then it says: when you see this with wisdom, you grow weary of suffering, you turn away from it, and that is the path to purity. Notice the order. Not first stop caring.
Not first pretend it didn't matter. First, see it clearly: this was put together, so it can come apart.
The cake, the file, the drawing, and also the anger that rises when they're ruined. That rises and passes too. The seeing comes before the turning.

And the verse doesn't stand alone. The next two lines in the Dhammapada say all formations are suffering, and all things are not-self, each with the same ending: see it with wisdom, and you turn from suffering.

teach.h: THREE VERSES, ONE WAY OF LOOKING.
teach.b: Three verses, one way of looking. Yesterday's line was a sigh over a loss.
Today's line is a lens for a Tuesday: sabbe sankhara anicca.

how: Theravada chanting books include sabbe sankhara anicca and its two companion lines, and teachers give the three as a way of looking at anything that changes.

o: all things put together are impermanent
all good things come back in time
all things that pass are meaningless

games.q: three verses, one way of looking — tap the pairs.
p: see it with wisdom, turn from suffering

s: the verse tells you to stop caring about things
it asks you to see clearly that formations pass; seeing comes first, then turning from suffering.
Dhammapada 277 has companion verses after it
the next two say all formations are suffering, and all things are not-self.
the verse covers all formations: a cake, a file, a drawing, a flash of anger.

games.q: you spend a week on a project and it gets deleted. by Dhammapada 277, what's the first move?
o: see it clearly: it was put together, so it could come apart.
act as if it never mattered to you, so the loss can't sting.
find whose fault it was, so the loss at least makes sense.
games.why: the verse's order is see, then turn: when you see with wisdom that formations are impermanent, you turn from suffering. it never asks you to pretend you didn't care.

practice: Let your eyes move slowly around the room and land on one thing at a time: a mug, the light on a wall, your own hand. With each one, say quietly, sabbe sankhara anicca, and just look, without needing to feel anything about it.
When you've looked enough, let your eyes rest and sit.

wordCard.voice: All formations pass. Sabbe sankhara anicca: all things put together are impermanent. See it, and you turn from suffering. Word fourteen of a little Pali.

orig.note: sabbe sankhara anicca in Devanagari letters: all formations are impermanent (Dhammapada 277).

carryVoice: Your line for today: sabbe sankhara anicca, a lens to see through, not a shrug. Fourteen down.

sources.ref: Dhammapada 277–279 (sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā; sabbe saṅkhārā dukkhā; sabbe dhammā anattā: when one sees with wisdom, one turns from suffering; this is the path to purity)
